abstract: Manganese is essential for immunity and neurological health, and its dysregulation causes Parkinsonism and dystonia. We present cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of human ZnT10, a Mn 2+ /Zn 2+ transporter, in symmetric inward-facing and asymmetric inward/outward states. Conformational shifts in TM1, TM2, TM4, and TM5, along with rearranged protomer interactions, control substrate access. Structural analysis reveals the substrate-binding sites for Mn 2+ and endogenous Zn 2+ in ZnT10. Molecular dynamic simulation also provides supportive evidence for the ion coordination. Mn 2+ transitions between distinct coordination sites during conformational changes, whereas Zn 2+ remains bound in the same pocket. Radial distribution functions (RDF) indicate that Zn 2+ requires more water coordination, making it a less preferred substrate. These results clarify the molecular basis of metal recognition and selectivity in ZnT10, providing key insights into manganese specificity determinants.

title: Structures of distinct human acetylcholinesterase tetramer forms in complex with synaptic anchoring proteins
abstract: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) hydrolyzes the neurotransmitter acetylcholine in the nervous system. Higher order oligomeric forms of AChE are specific to synapses in vertebrates. The enzyme is anchored to the basal lamina at neuromuscular junctions by ColQ and to neuronal membranes in the brain by the membrane protein PRiMA. We use cryo-electron microscopy to show that human AChE (hAChE) forms distinct tetramers in complex with the two synaptic anchors. The ColQ complex is more compact and square-like while the PRiMA complex is more open, asymmetric, and flexible. 3D variability analysis also reveals different flexibilities within the complexes, which are also different than AChE tetramers from other species. Binding of hAChE to the anchors occurs through a conserved mechanism but differences within the anchor sequences may lead to significantly different structures. Flexibility of hAChE tetramer form may be important for interactions with endogenous proteins in the nervous system.

title: Chaperoning by dynamic encasement: Structural basis of linker histone H1 nuclear import
abstract: Importins transport numerous proteins into cell nuclei. They also chaperone highly positively charged cargoes against ionic aggregation during transit. An extreme example is histone H1, which requires two importins, Importin 7 (Imp7) and Importin β (Impβ), for safe import. Here, we present a combined cryoelectron microscopy (cryo-EM)/molecular dynamics (MD) structure of the Imp7·Impβ·H1 complex, correcting a previous model (PDB 6N88) with misassigned importin chains. Our structure reveals that Imp7 contacts Impβ via three interfaces and that this heterodimerization creates a large negatively charged cavity. The globular H1-domain is recognized by Imp7 alone. The highly cationic C-terminal H1-tail participates in fluid-like transient interactions, contacting the inner surface of Impβ before returning to the α-solenoid and long acidic loop of Imp7. This architecture and dynamics explain how the importins shield the histone's enormous positive charge while avoiding interactions too strong for efficient intranuclear cargo release. Finally, we report a RanGTP·Imp7 structure, illustrating how RanGTP dissociates the import complex inside nuclei.

title: Virulence gene regulation in Pseudomonas aeruginosa is mediated by a novel hinge motion in the signaling helix of GacS histidine kinase
abstract: Sensor kinases (SKs) play central roles in bacterial adaptation to environmental challenges. Signal perception by these membrane-embedded enzymes initiates phosphotransfer cascades that regulate gene expression through cognate transcription factors. Although SKs were thought to function independently, interwoven multi-kinase networks have revealed a more complex picture. The present study focuses on GacS, a major regulator of virulence gene expression in the opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation revealed a novel hinge motion within the GacS S-helix region that is hypothesized to facilitate the interactions of GacS with RetS, another histidine kinase family protein that inhibits GacS. In vitro and in situ data support the functional importance of this flexible region for GacS-RetS interactions. Analysis of MD data also provided striking insights into conformational coupling between domains and into how GacS-RetS interactions might be regulated to modulate P. aeruginosa virulence gene expression.

title: Reconstructing hidden GPCR conformations and ligand binding modes through integrative DEER modeling
abstract: Binding of biased ligands to a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) stabilizes specific receptor conformations, leading to distinct physiological responses. Recently, intra-transducer bias has emerged as an additional mechanism that fine-tunes receptor function by stabilizing specific architectures of the receptor-transducer complex. This mechanism was demonstrated for the angiotensin receptor (AT1R) and its β-arrestin-biased ligand TRV026, which selectively promotes β-arrestin-1 engagement via the receptor C terminus while preventing interaction with the receptor core. Here, we present a computational protocol integrating double electron-electron resonance (DEER) data with deep learning-based structure prediction and molecular dynamics simulations to reconstruct all-atom models of TRV026-bound AT1R. Using a new clustering method, we identify key ligand-receptor interactions underlying high-affinity binding, localized receptor flexibility, and ligand bias. Our results provide a framework for validating neural-network predictions and physics-based simulations to capture rare signaling states of membrane proteins and identify target conformations for designing more functionally selective, efficacious therapeutics.

title: Q&A with Christopher O. Barnes
abstract: In this Q&A, Structure's editor-in-chief, Karin Kühnel, speaks with Christopher O. Barnes, assistant professor at Stanford University and Freeman Hrabowski Scholar from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, about his research and his involvement in efforts to support African-led cryo-EM research teams.

title: A missing piece of the WFC trafficking complex revealed by cryo-EM
abstract: In this issue of Structure, Zhang et al. 1 report high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the human WDR11-FAM91A1-C17orf75 complex, establishing C17orf75 as an integral core subunit and revealing the molecular basis by which this ternary machinery coordinates retrograde vesicle tethering and selective sorting of super-acidic-cluster-containing cargoes.

title: Meet the author: Nadia Izadi-Pruneyre
abstract: In this meet-the-author Q&A, we speak with Nadia Izadi-Pruneyre from the Institut Pasteur and CNRS in Paris about her work and career; her research group's recent Structure paper, "Structural determinants of endopilus assembly, stability, and functional specificity in bacterial type II secretion"; and the collaborative effort behind this study.

title: Molecular mechanism of KRAS binding to BRAF and its regulation by the BRAF-specific region
abstract: MAPK pathway activation requires recruitment of RAF kinases by GTP-bound RAS through the RAS-binding domain (RBD) and cysteine-rich domain (CRD). BRAF uniquely contains an N-terminal BRAF-specific region (BSR), but the structural basis of KRAS engagement and BSR function remain unclear. Here, we report the structure of KRAS bound to BRAF(RBD-CRD) and compare it with KRAS-CRAF(RBD-CRD). Although the RBD engages KRAS through a conserved mechanism, the BRAF(CRD) adopts a hinge-like displacement away from KRAS, forming fewer contacts and contributing less to binding than CRAF(CRD). Structural analysis, biophysical measurements, and AlphaFold3 modeling show that the BSR does not directly contact KRAS but instead regulates RBD accessibility through a cis-acting mechanism that requires linkage to the RBD. Without the CRD, the BSR-RBD linker restricts KRAS binding, whereas CRD inclusion stabilizes BSR positioning and partially relieves inhibition. Disease-associated mutations further support a regulatory role for BRAF(CRD), defining an isoform-specific mechanism regulating RAF activation.

title: Structural analysis of de novo-designed binders targeting the closed state of HSP90
abstract: Heat shock protein 90 (HSP90) assists the folding and maturation of numerous signaling proteins and is an important therapeutic target. Most HSP90 inhibitors target the ATP-binding pocket and disrupt ATP-induced closure, whereas inhibitors targeting the closed state have not been developed. Here, we report de novo-designed protein binders that selectively recognize closed HSP90. Two binders, H2 and H4, have similar folds and affinities for HSP90 but distinct binding kinetics. Cryo-EM structures of HSP90 complexes with H2 and H4 revealed high accuracy of the BindCraft predictions. H2 and H4 compete with p23 at one, but not both, symmetrical p23-binding sites. In HEK293T cells, H2 induced a reduced heat shock response compared with the ATP-site inhibitor 17-DMAG while reducing levels of CDK4, providing functional evidence for HSP90 inhibition. These binders provide tools for probing HSP90 function and potential leads for developing closed-state HSP90 inhibitors.

title: Cryo-EM structure of the Arabidopsis thaliana V-type ATPase
abstract: V-ATPases couple ATP hydrolysis in their cytosolic V 1 region to proton translocation through their membrane-embedded V O region to acidify the lumen of organelles. Functional diversity in the pump is enabled by tissue- and organelle-specific expression of paralogous genes for its subunits. Interactions between V-ATPase and TLDc domain-containing proteins regulate the enzyme in yeast and mammals but their relevance in plants is unclear. We isolated V-ATPase from Arabidopsis thaliana and determined its structure by electron cryomicroscopy. Mass spectrometry showed that most of the enzyme originated from the tonoplast. The structural analysis revealed three main rotational states, and structural and biochemical experiments showed S-acylation of subunits AP1 and the tonoplast-specific subunit a3 isoform. A subpopulation of complexes derived from the trans-Golgi network/early endosome was bound to the TLDc protein OXR5. These findings reveal plant-specific V-ATPase features and suggest organelle-specific interactions with TLDc proteins, pointing to conserved but context-dependent V-ATPase regulation in eukaryotes.

title: ERIS2: A deep-learning platform for predicting mutation-induced protein stability changes
abstract: Accurately predicting changes in protein thermodynamic stability upon mutation is a fundamental challenge in protein engineering and therapeutics. Deep learning has improved prediction, but many models remain limited by small, imbalanced training data and poor generalization across mutation types. Here, we present ERIS2, an attention-convolutional deep learning framework that integrates contextual sequence embeddings with atomistic and residue-level structural features from experimental protein structures to predict mutation-induced stability changes. Trained on large-scale experimental measurements combined with curated ProTherm data, a 5-fold ERIS2 ensemble achieved Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.69 on S461, 0.51 on S669, and 0.60 on S96, three blind-test datasets sequence-disjoint from all training configurations, and showed negligible anti-symmetry bias on Ssym forward and reverse pairs. ERIS2 is freely available as a structure-based web server without registration, providing a robust framework for protein stability prediction and advancing computational tools for protein engineering and therapeutic design.
